titleStmt.title: Dynamic replacement of software in hard real-time systems

analytic.title: Dynamic replacement of software in hard real-time systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: There are systems that cannot be stopped without losses. However, these systems require modifications during their operational life. Dynamic software replacement is a mechanism that allows components updating without stopping the whole system.

This paper deals with dynamic replacement in hard real-time systems. A protocol for dynamic replacement of software components in embedded hard realtime systems was described and proved theoretically. I n order to assess it practically, an implementation of the most critical aspects of this protocol has been carried out. Special attention has been devoted to ensure that the protocol does not interfere with the fulfillment of the deadlines of the real-time processes and that the schedulability test can be applied.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Recent advances in priority-based real-time systems have resulted in a set of protocols and implementation guidelines that allows their utilization in industrial applications. The Rate Monotonic Analysis (RMA) [13] and Deadline Monotonic Analysis (DMA) [5] methods are two pieces of theory that illustrate the above statement. However, it is also clear that more research *The work reported in this paper has been supported by the Spanish National Research Program on Production Technologies, project no. TAP-93-00001-CP is needed to extend their use to some application areas where those methods cannot be applied in a fully satisfactory way. Highly dynamic systems are a clear example of them.

The same holds for non-stop real-time systems, which main feature is that they cannot be stopped due to safety or service availability reasons. Space applications with long operational life or telecommunication systems with very low fault rates (few hours in a year), are examples of this kind of systems.

In this scenario, an important problem arises: these systems must evolve, due to changes in the environment or in the system requirements that cannot be entirely predicted during the design, or due to misbehaving software modules. Then, the traditional maintenance technique, consisting on stopping the whole system, installing the new version, and finally resuming system execution, is no longer valid.

The alternative is to develop a system where parts of the code can be dynamically replaced, while the rest of the system continues working. Several efforts has been devoted to deal with that issue [3] [12] [ll].

However, none of these approaches addresses the problem of dynamic replacement in hard real-time systems. A dynamic replacement protocol that considers the fulfillment of hard deadlines during that operation has been presented and theoretically proved in [2].

The purpose of this paper is to present an implementation of this protocol, in order to asses it. It should be noted that due to practical problems only some of the protocol phases have been implemented. However, the work that is presented deals with the most critical parts of the protocol.

The spiral process model [6] [7] was used in order to guide the development and to reduce the associated risks. It has been very useful and has allowed to op-timize the effort. The design and implementation will be presented from this perspective.

In section 2, a brief introduction to the dynamic replacement protocol is provided. Section 3 presents the general approach followed and the main issues of the implementation. The description of an application used for assessing the functional behaviour of the protocols is shown in section 4. An analysis of the timing behaviour is included in section 5. Finally, section 6 contains the conclusions of this paper.

div.head: Dynamic Replacement Protocol
div.p: The purpose of this section is to give a short presentation of the replacement protocol. However, due to lack of the space it is not possible to present all the details. The protocol is explained in depth in [2].

div.head: System Model
div.p: This section establishes the basic assumptions and underlying concepts of this work. The real-time system model follows the priority-based scheduling theory. In this model, the system is centralized, based on priorities and consists of a set of periodic and sporadic processes with hard deadlines. According to the scheduling method, higher priorities are assigned to the process with shorter deadlines (DMA). In this framework, process deadlines are guaranteed provided that processor utilization is below a known limit, that depends on processes attributes [5].

The communication is based on the client-server model. In this approach, servers are monitors that execute services with mutual exclusion and according to the priority ceiling protocol [l]. The processes communicate by message passing and there is no memory sharing. This configuration implies that the system is logically distributed, although it is not physically distributed. This characteristic simplifies the replacement protocol and its adaptation to physically distributed systems.

Within this method, certain support for system adaptation to dynamic changes is provided by the ability to change the execution mode [13]. However, as these changes must be considered during t,he design, the mode change protocol is not the the solution to deal with modifications in the system specification in non-stop systems.

div.head: The Replacement Unit
div.p: The first goal when dealing with dynamic replacement is to determine the minimum replaceable unit. The replacement unit that we consider to be most convenient is the process. It is a meaningful entity in the model and its size is adequate. It completely encapsulates its internal strate, makes no reference to any shared component having an internal state and communicates through clearly defined interfaces.

div.head: Requirements for System Components
div.p: The components involved in replacement protocol must fulfill a set of basic requirements:

e Operating system. In addition to the functionality required by the scheduling method, the operating system must provide some additional features, that are not commonplace in real-time operating systems:
-Dynamic creation and deletion of processes:

As the replacing unit is the process, whenever a replacement operation is going to be issued, the replacing unit must be created, and the replaced unit must be deleted, if the operation is successful.

-Dynamic memory management: During the operational life of the system, several replacement operations would take place. It is necessary to dynamically manage the memory for allocating new processes and collecting the memory freed by the deleted processes.

e Replacement supervisor. A dynamically replaceable system requires some management functions, as communicating with the remote system that decides when and what should be replaced, loading and creating the replacing unit, etc. In our model, a special process, the replacement supervisor, is responsible for them. It can be viewed as a sporadic process, as only executes in response to an event.

It has been proved that, under the schedulability point of view, the behaviour of a sporadic server is equivalent to a periodic process with the same period and budget [14] and, consequently, the replacement supervisor can be included in the analysis in the same way that the rest of system pro- cesses.
SWRU. From a functional point of view, a SWRU (Software Replaceable Unit) is composed of two parts.

-One component achieves the actual functionality of the unit. Its internal state is represented by a data structure called checkpoint data. Within this code, a set of points where this information is consistent can be identified.

-The other component embodies the replacement protocol. When the execution of the unit reaches a consistent point, it is checked if there is a replacement request for that SWRU. In that case, the replaced unit sends the checkpoint data to the replacing one. In this way, the later starts form the same state than the former.

The general structure of a real-time process is a portion of code that is continuously executed in response to the expiration of a delay or to the occurrence of an event. In this case, the obvious consistent point is the end of an activation.

It is important to note that one requirement of the protocol is that the execution time required by the replacing and the replaced unit to interchange the checkpoint data must be taken into account in the schedulability analysis. This can be made by adding this time to the computation time of the highest priority process. This is enough because dynamic replacements cannot take place simultaneously. The alternative will be to add t,his time to every process, but this will waste computation capacity.

div.head: Dynamic Replacement Protocol
div.p: The detailed sequence of replacement operations is as follows:
Loading phase.

1. The supervisor receives an external replace-2. It request the operating system to allocate memory for the replacing unit, and then starts to load the replacing unit. This load is performed in time slices, in accordance to its execution budget. ment command.
Creation phase.
The supervisor creates the process of the replacing unit.

The initialization code of the replacing unit is executed with the execution profile of the supervisor. This means that the used computation time is part of the budget assigned to the supervisor. In this way there is no disturbance to other processes.
When the replacing unit is ready to execute the replacement operation, it changes its priority to the same value than the replaced unit and blocks.
6. The supervisor communicates to the replaced unit that it is going to be replaced and that it should to execute the replacement procedure.

When the replaced unit reaches a consistent state, it sends its state information to the replacing unit 8. The replaced unit sends the status of the replacement to the supervisor.
9. The replacing unit executes at the next activation time, if the state is received properly.
10. If the operation is executed correctly, the replaced unit ends. In other case, it will execute in the next activation.

div.head: Design and Implementation Issues
div.p: After defining the protocol for the dynamic replacement of software, the next step was to implement it. In this way it could be possible to create replaceable systems. The goals were to assess practically the viability of the protocol and to develop a set of components and guidelines to assist in the development of these kind of systems. This paper concentrates in the first point.

The protocol should be tested from two different points of view: 0 Functional behaviour: The processes must fulfill their functional requirements during and after a replacement operation. In particular, the following issues should be checked when such an operation is performed:
-Transparency: Those units that are not directly involved in the replacement, should not be aware of the execution of this operation.
-Units consistency: The replacement operation has to be performed when the replaced unit is in a consistent state, i.e. there are no pending activities and data is stable.
-Conservation of the execution state: The new unit should not start from scratch. It must consider the status of the replaced unit.
0 Timing behaviour: Real-time processes must meet their deadlines during and after a replacement operation.

In the remainder of the section the design and implementation choices taken for implementing the dynamic replacement protocol [SI are presented. The assessment of the protocol is shown in later sections.

div.head: Overall Approach
div.p: We have followed the spiral model [6] [7] for phnning the different stages in the development of this project. The risk-driven approach, its flexibility, and its simple integration with prototyping and reusing, has allowed us to optimize our effort.
In the development of the system four spiral rounds have been spent:
1. Firstly a feasibility study was performed. The suitability of different platforms, operating systems, and tools for developing the protocol were studied.
A first prototype was developed for checking the functional behaviour of the implementation. As part of this round, a first version of communication mailboxes was developed.
In the second prototype the units and mailboxes were enhanced to deal with faults in the operations.

Finally, the timing behaviour of the implementation was carefully checked. For this purpose, code that generates execution traces was added to the application. In addition, minor adjustments were made to the implementation of the protocol.

div.head: Selection of Implementation Platform
div.p: Initially, a feasibility study was performed for evaluating the suitability of different execution kernels
(POSIX [lo] and Ada [4]). None of them provides the required functionality (dynamic loading of processes and dynamic memory management). POSIX

does not provide an standard way for dealing with dynamic memory. It relies on the specific languages for this purpose. Ada does not meet any of these two functional requirements. On the other hand, the possibility of developing an appropriate kernel from scratch was discarded, due to the required effort.

As it was not possible to implement completely the protocol with the available platforms, it was decided to concentrate our effort in the most critical phases: creation and replacement. To overcome the problem of the missed functionality, it was supposed that the replacing unit had been created, and then the communication with the system supervisor and the replacement phase was implemented. The phases selected are the most innovative. Hence, phases ranging between number four and number twelve have been the core of the development. The other phases either can be implemented in a straightforward way with the current technology or the associated problems will be solved with the appropriate platform.

The selected implementation platform was Ada, running in a MVME-135 embedded computer. This platform meets the requirements of being an embedded computer, providing sufficient time granularity and being robust enough.

div.head: Communications Model
div.p: One of the requirements of the protocol is that communication should be based on an indirect mechanism. This implies that messages are not interchanged directly by the sender and the receiver. An intermediate object is used where messages are written and read. This mechanism eases the execution of replacement operations, because it is possible to replace the sender or the receiver, without interfering with the execution of other intercommunicating agents.
Ada does not provide this communication mechanism. To overcome this problem communication objects, based on message passing and mailboxes, were developed.
The mailbox was implemented as a server task and based on the priority ceiling protocol.

In the first prototype, a simple communications model was chosen. General mailboxes were implemented for communication purposes, and then used for communicating the units involved in the replacement operation: supervisor, replaced unit and replacing unit (figure 1). Although this approach worked fine, the use of three mailboxes per replacing task introduces excessive overheads in the execution of the protocol. So, it was decided to develop specialized mailboxes to communicate the units during the replacement, gaining efficiency.

div.head: / m d r d I
div.p: In a later prototype (third round of the spiral), different mailboxes types were defined, to take advantage of the different requirements of the communications between units. In addition, timeouts were included to avoid blocking or excessive duration of the operation. The value of the timeout is dynamically set to the value of the deadline of the unit to be replaced. In this way, a fault in the replacement can be detected and handled in the same way as a deadline overrun.
Figure 2 shows a detailed design graphic, including the different types of mailboxes and the operations supported.

The NoticeJlailbox object is an enhanced version of Mailbox A, with addressing capabilities. In this way, the Replacing-Command is only received by the task whose identifier matches that included in the command. This mailbox is shared by all the replaceable units.

The InterchangeAailbox object is the result of a combination of Mailboxes B and C, and is also shared by all the replaceable units, as only one replacing operation happens at any time. This implies the standardization of the type of the state passed. The main novelties in its use are:

0 The replacing unit notifies the end of its initial code with Get-State and gets blocked in the mail- box. This operation ensures that thee unit is ready to receive the state as soon as it is delivered by the Replaced Unit.
0 Some entries were added to the mailbox for restarting the operation in case of malfunctioning (end of the deadline of the unit to be replaced, blocking, etc.).

div.head: Structure of the Supervisor
div.p: The Supervisor is implemented as a sporadic task [14]

[9]. Its priority and computation time is not fixed and depends on the attributes of the processes set for each application. If the duration, U , of one of the operations that it must execute is longer than the budget, c, it should be executed during n successive periods, where n.c 2 U.
The Supervisor will be normally blocked, waiting for a replacement request. Once it is issued, it is awakened and executes the the replacement protocol.

div.head: Structure of SWRU
div.p: A SWRU is implemented as a task. It includes an initialization routine that is executed when the unit is going to replace another one. This code provides the operations needed for initializing the unit, communicating the end of this operation to the supervisor and getting the checkpoint data from the replaced unit. The initialization operations are executed with the priority of the supervisor. The interchange of the state is performed with the priority of the replaced unit, that is the one that will be used for the execution of the task after the replacement operation.

Once that the replacement has been executed successfully, the SWRU will execute cyclically the appli-cation specific code. The activation of this cycle depends on the type of the task, that can be periodic or sporadic. At the end of each activation, the unit checks if a replacement command has been issued. In that case, the protocol is executed as mentioned.
The structure of the task should follow the protocol and the requirements of the scheduling method. Priority is assigned to the tasks and to the mailboxes following the Deadline Monotonic rules.

div.head: Assessment of the functional behaviour
div.p: In order to assess the behaviour of the implementation of the protocol practically two outstanding applications were developed: 0 Control of a model railroad: This system was mainly used for checking the functional behaviour of the protocol.

0 Simulation of a system with high requirements for computation time: It was used for checking the timing behaviour in an application with a pro- cessor utilization close to the schedulability limit. This development is presented and analyzed in section 5

The purpose of the first application is to control a pair of trains running in a model railroad. This is divided in a set of electrically isolated sections, that are powered independently. The application must ensure that there is only one train in each section, there are no collisions and each train follows a predefined path. A set of sensors are distribute along the tracks for detecting the position of the trains.

The timing requirements are related with the maximum allowed time needed to stop a train that is going to enter a section that may be taken by another train, the time to decide the next section of a train entering a cross, and the time needed to poll safely the sensors. The resultant system was composed by seven real-time processes, plus some background ones for monj toring and displaying the state of the model railroad.

The process in charge of rout,ing the trains and managing simultaneous requests for entering a section, was selected to be replaced. The change is related with the algorithm for managing simultaneous requests. Initially, priority was given to the trains in an arbitrary way. The replaced process will benefit the trains with higher speed.
The deadlines were met and no strange behaviour WEI S observed after

The replacement was successful. executing a high number of times this application. In this replacement was specially important to consider the replaced process state prior to the replacement operation. In other case, the control over the trains may be lost. In all the executions, the checkpoint data was transferred correctly and no undesirable b e haviour happened. Finally, it was checked that processes not involved in the replacement did not appear to notice it.

div.head: Timing Analysis
div.p: Due to the target systems of this protocol, special emphasis has to be made in the assessment of its timing behaviour. For this purpose, the execution time of the protocol was measured and a test application was developed. These aspects are dealt with in this section.

div.head: Time Accounting
div.p: In order to include the computational costs of the replacement operations in the schedulability analysis was necessary to carefully measure the worst-case execution time of the protocol. This time will be added to the computation time of the highest priority task, as noted above.

In our platform the time consumed in the replacement operation is around lms. The implementation of the mailboxes as tasks introduces additional context switches and reduces the efficiency of the protocol. The use of more appropriate language constructs, as the protected records in Ada 9X, will improve the protocol execution speed.

div.head: Assessment of the timing behaviour
div.p: In addition to the unit that were going to be replaced, in the last prototype a set of dummy tasks were included in order to simulate a load close to the maximum processor capability. In this way, the protocol were tested in a scenario were possible faults could be detected.

The assessment of the timing behaviour was based on traces generated during execution that are stored in memory and then extracted when the application ends. The overhead that this method implies is negligible and was, by far, the best available alternative.

Their analysis has allowed to have a precise image of the events that occurs during the execution of the system. The granularity of the time in the platform ( 6 1 ~s ) allows a high precision in this measurements.
In the rest of the section some figures with the timing of the protocol are shown. Only the traces of the events of the units involved in a replacement operation are included.

A view of the sequence of operations is in figure 3. The replaced unit has a period of 200ms and a computation time of approximately 50ms. In time 15.0s, the replacing unit starts the replacement operations. It notifies this fact to the supervisor, which signals this event to the replaced unit. When the replaced unit ends its activation, it starts t.0 execute the replacement protocol. It can be seen that after interchanging the state, the replacing task executes the activation in 15.2s, instead of the replaced one. 1. The unit to be replaced completes the execution of its functional code and look at the notice mailbox.
2. It processes the request, sending to the calling unit a message with the indication that it is going to be replaced.
The unit to be replaced gets the message and sends its state.
The interchange mailbox passes it to the replacing unit.
This unit receives it and sends an acknowledge.

'Time intervals when no task executes represent operations performed by the run-time system 6 . The interchange mailbox receives the acknowledge and reports to the supervisor the result of the operation.

The replaced unit ends and the replacing continues executing. It is important to note that in the figures, the supervisor executes for a large amount of time. This is due to some textual messages sent to a console for monitoring purposes.

It can be checked in these figures that the replacement phase behaves as the theoretical protocol. The computation time spent by the replacing and replaced units is taken into account in the schedulability analysis. It should be noted that the replacement operation by the replaced and replacing units is executed without delays. In this way the requirements imposed by the scheduling method are met.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: The dynamic replacement of software is an important feature to ensure the continuous operation of nonstop systems when it is necessary to modify parts of them. Although the dynamic replacement protocol for embedded real-time systems has been theoretically (ts- sessed, no practical implementations have been carried out.

In the work reported, the most critical parts of the protocol have been implemented and carefully tested. In particular, specific communication mailboxes, the SWRU and the replacement supervisor have been developed. The functional and timing behaviour of the implementation have been successfully checked. The computation time of the protocol has been measured in order to allow the development of system composed by SWRU's that can be analyzed using the schedula-
